assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 14,822 ops/s at peak (a Friday dinner rush in one large market), of which 52/s are actual orders. The order rate is DERIVED from the request budget, not asserted: the previous version claimed 900 orders/s at 15,000 rps, which contradicted its own stated ping/poll cadences by one to two orders of magnitude (900 orders/s x a 15-minute delivery is 810,000 deliveries in flight, which at one customer poll per 5 s is 162,000 polls/s alone — 43x the 3,750 it allocated). We kept the ~15,000 rps budget and solved for the order rate, because that keeps every component size in this file teachable; the alternative (keep 900 orders/s and let system_rps rise to 150,000-400,000) describes a different, much larger system.

assumptions.subject: mix-derivation
assumptions.statement: The flow shares are Little's Law on the cadences, not a guess. 52 orders/s x 900 s door-to-door = 46,800 deliveries in flight. At one customer poll per 5 s that is 9,360 polls/s. At 3 orders batched per courier trip those deliveries are carried by 15,600 couriers on-job, and at one ping per 4 s that is 3,900 pings/s. Add 25 browse/search requests and 4 status reads per order (1,300/s and 208/s), the 52 order placements themselves, and 2 dispatch solves/s: 14,822 rps. Tracking is therefore ~89% of all requests. That shape is corroborated by Uber Engineering's real-time push platform post (uber.com/blog/real-time-push-platform): 'At some point, 80% of requests made to the backend API gateway were polling calls.'

assumptions.subject: scale
assumptions.statement: 52 orders/s in a single market is LARGE — DoorDash's Q4-2023 8-K (SEC EDGAR, 15 Feb 2024) reports 'Total Orders increased 23% Y/Y to 574 million' for the quarter, about 72 orders/s worldwide on average and perhaps 220-360/s at global peak. Read this blueprint as a deliberately big single-metro teaching case, not as a company-wide figure.

assumptions.subject: delivery-duration
assumptions.statement: 15 minutes door-to-door (order placed -> delivered) is an ASSUMPTION; no operator publishes this distribution. It is the single most load-bearing input in the mix: at 30 minutes every in-flight count, and therefore every poll and ping rate, doubles for the same order rate.

assumptions.subject: courier-batching
assumptions.statement: 3 orders carried simultaneously per courier trip is an ASSUMPTION — no public figure exists for stacked-order rates. Courier ping volume moves inversely with it: unbatched (1 order per trip) the same 52 orders/s would offer 11,700 pings/s instead of 3,900.

assumptions.subject: browse-per-order
assumptions.statement: 25 browse/search requests and 4 status reads per completed order are ASSUMPTIONS, not measured figures; they stand in for the majority of sessions that browse and never convert. No food-delivery operator publishes a session-to-order request ratio.

assumptions.subject: track
assumptions.statement: Couriers ping roughly every 4 s while on a job and customers poll every 5 s while waiting. Both go to Redis, not to PostgreSQL — persisting every GPS point to the database is the classic way this design falls over.

assumptions.subject: dispatch
assumptions.statement: Assignment is a PERIODIC BATCH SOLVE on a timer, not a per-request service. DoorDash's deployed dispatch paper (Wu, Hou & Xie, arXiv:2606.13604v1) describes 'a combinatorial assignment optimizer' covering 'approximately 4,000 geographic regions', 'serving hundreds of millions of daily inferences at a 20-second cadence', where 'The system executes approximately three runs per minute'. This single metro is modelled as 40 zones x 3 solves per minute = 2 solves/s. One unit of load on this component is ONE ZONE SOLVE covering every pending order in that zone — at 52 orders/s over 2 solves/s that is ~26 assignments per solve, which is why the solve fans out 26 writes to the database and 26 assignment events to the bus rather than making one request each.

assumptions.subject: dispatch-model
assumptions.statement: HONESTY CAVEAT, same class as the streaming one below: assignment is modelled here as a request service because that is the only shape this engine has. Real dispatch is a periodic combinatorial solve whose cost tracks REGION COUNT and QUEUE DEPTH, not arrival rate — so the lever a reader reaches for on this component should be the solve cadence, the zone size and how long assignment is deliberately delayed to batch, NOT the instance count. Delay is a feature, not a fault: the same DoorDash paper's switchback test measured batching at +0.495 percentage points (p<0.001) all-day and +0.600 pp (p=0.010) at dinner. Treat this component's utilisation as 'are there enough solver workers to finish every zone within one cadence', and nothing more.

assumptions.subject: dispatch-solve-time
assumptions.statement: ~2 s per zone solve is an ASSUMPTION and the weakest number in this file. NO public per-solve time exists for any production assignment optimiser, because real ones are not sized in requests per second at all. The previous version's 350 assignments/s per instance at 40 ms is the one figure here that a primary source actively contradicts, and it was what made dispatch the named bottleneck.

assumptions.subject: dispatch-cost
assumptions.statement: Dispatch is the largest compute line in this design while being a rounding error in request count (2 solves/s out of 14,822). That is the point: the optimiser is bought in worker-hours to hold a cadence, not in capacity to absorb traffic.

assumptions.subject: search
assumptions.statement: Discovery is the heaviest read path (~25 ms per query: geo filter, ranking, availability), which is why search carries more instances than the order service despite lower traffic than tracking.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Real-time map streaming to the customer app is modelled as POLLING, because streaming/push is outside Keystone v1 scope. A WebSocket implementation would move that load from request rate to concurrent connections and change the tracking tier's sizing.

assumptions.subject: search-headroom
assumptions.statement: Discovery is deliberately left with headroom instead of being sized to the 85% ceiling: at the ceiling the same 25 ms query would spend several times its own service time waiting in queue, and search latency is what customers experience as the app being slow.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: Single PostgreSQL primary for orders and reference data — a single point of failure. Menus and courier positions are cached, so it sees only a small fraction of total request volume: courier pings never reach it at all, and the 9,360 polls/s reach it only on a 5% cache-miss path.

assumptions.subject: bottleneck-naming
assumptions.statement: Before this correction the engine named the dispatch engine over the tracking tier by a margin far smaller than the uncertainty on either component's per_instance_rps — both of which are uncited guesses, because no operator publishes app-tier capacity figures. A named bottleneck is only worth acting on when it leads by more than that error bar; the engine reports its own margin and lists joint contenders, so read that line before spending money on the component it names.

assumptions.subject: capacity-provenance
assumptions.statement: The per_instance_rps and base_latency_ms values for gw, track, search, order and dispatch are ASSUMPTIONS. Only the Redis figure has outside support — Lyft's RedisConf17 deck (Daniel Hochman) reports 10-15M QPS across '50 clusters with a total of 750 instances', roughly 15-20k rps per instance, and the geo-index pattern modelled here is literally theirs ('pipeline.zset(geohash, user_id, now_seconds())' with a zremrangebyscore expiry). Every component in this file keeps provenance ASSUMPTION for exactly that reason: a priced component is not a measured one.

_library.summary: Ordering, courier dispatch and live delivery tracking for a food-delivery marketplace.
